newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CLAIMS THAT PROTESTORS TARGETED FEMALE POLICE
Federal Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says the ACTU should reverse its refusal to take responsibility for the August riots at Parliament House.
His comments follow claims that protestors targeted female police.
Mr Reith says an extensive article in the Australian Federal Police Association journal says the mob deliberately targetted policewomen.
He says the article would sicken most Australians.
Mr Reith says in light of the claims, he can't see how union leaders such as Jennie George can stay silent, while criticising the impact of the Government's workplace policies on women.
AIR NEW ZEALAND STRIKES NEW ALLIANCE
Air New Zealand says its new alliance with US carrier, United Airlines, will be a major boost for tourism in the region.
The alliance further strengthens Air New Zealand's place in the international market, after its purchase of a 50 per cent stake in Ansett Australia earlier this year.
Under the deal with United, the two airlines will operate code-share flights, share ground facilities and offer one stop check-ins, streamlined transfers and joint frequent flyer point credits.
HOWARD SAYS TO MAKE RECOMMENDATION ON PEOPLE'S CONVENTION BY YEAR'S END
Prime Minister, John Howard, has told Coalition MPs he hopes to put to them Cabinet's recommendations about the people's convention on the republic before the end of the year.
There are signs the Government is likely to abandon the election promise for half of the representatives to the convention to be elected, following concerns about the cost.
Mr Howard has told the Party Room, Cabinet consideration of the convention hasn't been completed.
ALSTON'S HOLIDAY?
The Federal Opposition has accused Communications Minister Richard Alston of wasting taxpayers' money on a trip he's planning to Britain and the United States over Christmas.
Senator Alston intends speaking with overseas experts on media rules, and pay-television cabling in London, New York and Los Angeles.
The ALP claims Senator Alston has meetings arranged for only two of his five days in New York, and is virtually doing no work during a stop-over in Hawaii on the way home.
But Senator Alston has told Parliament his New York schedule has yet to be worked out, and he'll be attending a very important media conference in Honolulu.
ANTIBODIES GROWN IN CULTURES
Immunologists from Asia and the Pacific region, meeting in Adelaide, have heard about the advantages of producing antibodies, without using animals, such as mice.
Instead, they're produced by cells grown in culture.

Head of Antibody Production at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Centre in New York, Howard Petrie, says the technique's been tried elswhere in the world, including Australia, but not on the same scale.
Antibodies are being used increasingly in the diagnosis and treatment of diseases.
HIGH COURT SAYS STATES CAN'T PASS LAWS THAT BIND COMMONWEALTH
The High Court has been told that States do not have Constitutional power to pass any laws which bind the Commonwealth.
The Full Bench in Canberra is currently hearing a challenge to the validity of the New South Wales Residential Tenancy Tribunal Act over the Defence Housing Authority.
The Authority is seeking a Writ of Prohibition against the Residential Tenancy Tribunal on the basis it has no power over Commonwealth agents.
The matter arises from a dispute over provision of a key to a Defence Force house which the Authority leased from a third party.
All the States have intervened to support New South Wales against the Defence Force Housing Authority and the Commonwealth.
FORMER RESERVE BANK HEAD FINDS WORK
The former Reserve Bank Governor, Bernie Fraser, has been appointed to the boards of three major national industry superannuation funds.
Mr Fraser, whose term at the Reserve Bank expired earlier this year, will serve as a trustee with the Superannuation Trust of Australia.
He'll also work for the Australian Retirement Fund, and C-BUS, the industry fund for the construction and building industries.
AGREEMENT HAILED AS A BREAKTHROUGH
A new industrial agreement between film and television producers, and performers is being hailed a major step forward for the industry.
An agreement covering pay and conditions for performers over the next three years has been finalised between the Screen Producers' Association and the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance.
It guarantees performers a 12 per cent wage increase over three years, and lifts a three-year embargo on showing Australian films on free-to-air television.
The Association's Geoff Brown says it means producers can plan projects years in advance and know what they'll have to pay performers.
Mr Brown says the agreement provides certainty.
MINING LEADER REJECTS ENTERPRISE CRITICISM
A mining union leader has rejected criticism of enterprise bargaining deals in Australia's black coal industry.

The Queensland President of the Miners' Union, Andrew Vickers, was replying to a study by the National Institute of Labour, which says a reluctance to accept enterprise reforms has left the industry lagging.
Mr Vickers says the federal award in question is a consent award, put into place by agreement between employers and the unions in 1990, and remaining there by agreement.
He also says it's ridiculous to complain about what is or isn't in enterprise agreements, when the agreement has been reached at the enterprise.
INSURANCE - CLAIMS STEADY, PAYOUTS UP
A survey by a national insurance company shows that burglars have moved on from their traditional booty of cash and jewellery.
The NRMA survey has found that more expensive goods are now being stolen, particularly electrical equipment.
It says although the number of claims did not increase last year, the NRMA paid out 12 per cent more in claims than in the year before in New South Wales and the ACT.
The payout totalled 37-million dollars, the increase equivalent to 63 dollars per policy holder.
The survey found the risk of theft is higher at Christmas.
AUSSIES TAKE TWO-NIL LEAD IN CRICKET SERIES
In cricket, Australia has won the second test against the West Indies at the SCG by 124 runs, to take a two-nil lead in the series.
Starting the day at none for 27, the West Indies, requiring 340 for victory, was dismissed for 215 .
For Australia much of the damage was done by Warne with four wickets, and McGrath who finished with three wickets.
For the Windies Chanderpaul made 71, and Hooper 57.
Glen McGrath was named man of the match.
